name: Alprazolam

binding.notes: Sanna et al. 2005 — comparator value for etizolam study.

binding.target: GABA-A α1β2γ2S (functional EC50 for GABA potentiation)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Classical benzodiazepine-site PAM: enhances GABA-driven Cl- influx through pentameric GABA-A. Triazole ring (1,2,4-triazolo annulation) confers higher intrinsic activity and contributes to its high potency and rapid tolerance development relative to 1,4-benzodiazepines.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults (Xanax FDA label / Greenblatt reviews)
routes.notes: Mean t1/2 ~11.2 h (range 6.3–26.9); F ≈ 90% IR tablet; protein binding ~80% (mostly albumin).

metabolism.notes: Schmider et al. — kinetic-dynamic study with erythromycin confirmed CYP3A4 as the major hydroxylation pathway. α-OH-alprazolam is roughly half as potent as parent in vivo.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: AUC ~3.98-fold increase, t1/2 prolonged from 12 h to 21 h
AUC decreased ~50%; reduces clinical effect substantially

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP3A4/5 polymorphisms modulate clearance; brain expression of CYP3A43 has been shown to generate active α-OH-alprazolam locally in human brain (Agarwal 2008).

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Triazolobenzodiazepines induce rapid tolerance to anticonvulsant/sedative effects within days–weeks at therapeutic doses; mechanism involves uncoupling of GABA-A allosteric site and α-subunit downregulation. No specific human in vivo half-time published.
cross_tolerance: all benzodiazepine-site agonists (clonazepam, diazepam, lorazepam, midazolam, Z-drugs)
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12–24 h (short t1/2); peak 1–4 days; total duration 4–8 weeks for somatic symptoms, months to years for protracted PAWS. Symptoms: rebound anxiety/insomnia, autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, perceptual distortions, seizures (high-dose discontinuation). Considered one of the more severe benzodiazepine withdrawal profiles due to short t1/2 + high potency.

demographic_differences.sex: Females show ~22% higher Cmax and lower CL than males (Greenblatt). Asians have ~15% lower CL than Caucasians per FDA label.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: CL reduced ~30%, t1/2 prolonged to ~16 h.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: t1/2 prolonged to ~19 h; reduce dose. Renal impairment: no significant change.

data_gaps_remaining: Subunit-specific Ki values (paper-by-paper they vary; classical view is non-selective)
notes: Triazolo ring confers higher intrinsic efficacy and faster tolerance development than 1,4-benzodiazepines like diazepam. Withdrawal severity at moderate doses is clinically significant due to short t1/2.

name: Diazepam

binding.tissue_or_cell: L(tk-) cells expressing recombinant human α1β2γ2
binding.notes: Hadingham et al. 1993 — canonical Ki values for human recombinant receptors. Classical 'non-selective' profile across α1/α2/α3/α5 with single-digit nM affinity.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prototypical non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM. Enhances GABA-A Cl- conductance by increasing channel-opening frequency at GABA-bound receptors. Roughly equal affinity across α1/α2/α3/α5; β-subunit identity has minor effect on diazepam Ki.

neuroimaging.finding: Brain occupancy of central benzodiazepine sites measured by [11C]flumazenil displacement reaches ~25% at 10 mg p.o.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults — Greenblatt clinical pharmacokinetics review
routes.notes: Parent t1/2 ~20–48 h; active metabolite nordazepam t1/2 50–100 h dominates effective duration on chronic dosing.

metabolism.notes: 3-hydroxylation
N-demethylation — primary route. Nordazepam t1/2 ~50–100 h; further metabolized to oxazepam (CYP3A4 hydroxylation) then UGT2B15-glucuronidated.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Decreased CL of diazepam by ~25–50% in CYP2C19 EMs (no effect in PMs)
Prolonged t1/2 and increased plasma levels

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs show ~2–4× higher diazepam AUC and prolonged t1/2 due to reduced N-demethylation. Substantial inter-individual variability in nordazepam accumulation.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Tolerance to sedative/anticonvulsant effects within 2–4 weeks; anxiolytic tolerance slower and incomplete. Mechanism includes α1-subunit-mediated uncoupling.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 2–10 days (long t1/2 due to nordazepam); milder/longer withdrawal than short-acting benzos. Symptoms: anxiety, insomnia, tremor, autonomic; rare seizures on abrupt discontinuation from high doses.

demographic_differences.sex: Females have slightly lower CL than males.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: CL reduced 50%, t1/2 doubled or more; nordazepam accumulation pronounced.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: marked t1/2 prolongation; cirrhosis triples t1/2. Renal: no major change in CL of parent but glucuronide metabolites accumulate.

notes: Reference 'classical' non-selective benzodiazepine. Active metabolite cascade (nordazepam → oxazepam) dominates pharmacology on chronic dosing.

name: Zolpidem

binding.notes: Hanson 2008. Zolpidem effectively does not bind α5-containing GABA-A — defining feature distinguishing it from eszopiclone.

receptor_oligomerisation.functional_consequence: Novel α1/α1 interface modulation discovered for zolpidem at low-γ stoichiometries; may contribute to abuse liability.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: α1-preferring imidazopyridine PAM. The α1G201 residue is the structural basis for selectivity (Pritchett & Seeburg 1991). Sedative-hypnotic action attributed almost exclusively to α1-containing receptors (KO-mouse studies; McKernan 2000).

neuroimaging.finding: [11C]flumazenil displacement at therapeutic doses shows ~25–30% global receptor occupancy at 10 mg.

routes.notes: Short t1/2 ~1.4–4.5 h; rapid onset (Tmax 1.6 h). Substantial first-pass.

metabolism.notes: All metabolites inactive at benzodiazepine site; carboxylic acid metabolites excreted renally.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Minor effect; CYP3A4/5 polymorphism alters CL but redundant pathways limit clinical impact.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Hypnotic tolerance modest at therapeutic doses for ≤4 weeks. Higher doses → tolerance and dependence resembling classical benzos.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset within hours of last dose (short t1/2); rebound insomnia, anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity. Seizures and delirium reported at supratherapeutic dependence.

demographic_differences.sex: Females have ~45% higher AUC than males at the same dose (FDA reduced female recommended dose to 5 mg in 2013).
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: Cmax +50%, half-life prolonged; max recommended dose 5 mg.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: CL reduced ~50%, t1/2 doubled.

notes: Prototype α1-selective Z-drug. Defining feature: no α5 affinity. Complex sleep-related behaviors (sleep-driving, sleep-eating) are FDA-recognized risk; female PK differences led to dose halving.

name: Eszopiclone

binding.notes: Note: eszopiclone retains α5 affinity unlike zolpidem — likely contributes to its memory/learning effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cyclopyrrolone PAM at benzodiazepine site. Similar to classical benzos in being non-selective across α1/α2/α3/α5 but lower absolute affinity. ~50× more potent than racemic zopiclone; R-enantiomer (dexzopiclone) is largely inactive.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~6 h. High-fat meal reduces Cmax by ~21% and prolongs Tmax to 2 h.

metabolism.notes: Minor activity at benzodiazepine site. (S)-zopiclone-N-oxide is the main inactive metabolite.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Limited tolerance to hypnotic effect over 6 months in clinical trials (a marketing claim, with caveats).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild relative to benzos at therapeutic doses; severe dependence reported in recreational misuse.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Characteristic metallic/bitter aftertaste (dysgeusia) is its most common side effect — occurs in ~34% of users and is thought to relate to salivary secretion of the parent drug.

demographic_differences.sex: No significant sex effect on PK.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: AUC 41% higher, t1/2 prolonged to 9 h; max recommended dose 2 mg.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment: AUC doubled; max 2 mg.

notes: Cyclopyrrolone Z-drug; structurally unrelated to benzos but binds the same site. Unlike zolpidem, retains α5 affinity → more amnesic/cognitive impact.

name: Lorazepam

binding.notes: Greenblatt clinical pharmacokinetics review (1981) — 2-amino-substituted 1,4-benzodiazepine with non-selective binding across α1/α2/α3/α5.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM with relatively high intrinsic activity. Lacks active metabolites (unlike diazepam) because metabolism is direct glucuronidation rather than CYP-mediated.

metabolism.notes: Both R- and S-lorazepam glucuronidated by UGT2B4, 2B7, 2B15. UGT2B15*2/*2 PMs show 40–50% lower lorazepam CL (Chung 2005, pmid:15961980).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Lorazepam CL reduced ~40%, plasma levels rise

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: UGT2B15*2/*2 homozygotes have 40–50% lower CL of lorazepam. No effect of CYP polymorphisms because lorazepam bypasses oxidative metabolism.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Tolerance develops similar to other benzos; absence of active metabolites means rebound effects are sharper.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12–24 h; peak 2–5 days; intermediate severity. Lack of long-acting metabolites means no 'self-tapering'; abrupt discontinuation more problematic.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: minor increases in t1/2; glucuronidation relatively preserved compared to CYP pathways.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: minimal change (glucuronidation preserved in cirrhosis). Renal impairment: glucuronide accumulates but inactive.

notes: Preferred benzo in hepatic dysfunction due to glucuronidation-only metabolism (also true for oxazepam and temazepam — 'LOT' rule). High binding affinity (~2 nM) at GABA-A relative to diazepam (~14 nM).

name: Midazolam

binding.notes: Imidazobenzodiazepine; pH-dependent ring-opening enables water solubility at acidic pH for IV/IM formulation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Imidazobenzodiazepine PAM; preferential occupancy of α1-containing receptors at sub-sedative concentrations (associated with anterograde amnesia). Used clinically as IV/IM sedative and probe drug for CYP3A4 activity (single highest-confidence in vivo CYP3A4 phenotyping substrate).

routes.notes: Extensive first-pass (CYP3A4 in gut wall and liver).

metabolism.notes: Kronbach 1989 / Gorski review; 1-OH-midazolam ≈ 20% of parent's BZ-receptor affinity. Active metabolite contributes to clinical effect, especially in renal failure where glucuronide can accumulate.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Oral AUC reduced >95%; renders midazolam nearly inactive orally

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP3A5 expressers (CYP3A5*1 carriers) clear midazolam ~25% faster than non-expressers. Population-level variability in CYP3A4 activity manifests as 5–10× variation in midazolam clearance — why midazolam is the gold-standard CYP3A4 probe substrate.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Tolerance develops rapidly with continuous IV infusion (days); rebound seizures reported on abrupt cessation.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Acute withdrawal on cessation of continuous infusion in ICU patients: agitation, seizures, tachycardia. Less commonly seen with single-dose use.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: CL reduced ~30%, t1/2 prolonged; neonates have very low CL (immature CYP3A).
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: prolonged t1/2 and reduced CL. Renal failure: 1-OH-midazolam glucuronide accumulates and contributes to prolonged sedation.

notes: Imidazobenzodiazepine designed for IV use — pH-dependent ring opens at pH <4 (water-soluble open form), closes at physiological pH (lipophilic active form). Massive intersubject variability in oral PK due to CYP3A4-dependent first pass.

name: Clonazepam

binding.notes: Sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar at all α subunits; among the highest-affinity classical benzodiazepines.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective high-affinity benzodiazepine-site PAM. The 7-nitro group is metabolically reduced to 7-amino-clonazepam — pharmacologically inactive in vivo but accumulates and may compete for binding after chronic dosing.

metabolism.notes: Nitroreduction to inactive 7-amino metabolite (major); minor 3-hydroxylation. 7-amino subsequently acetylated by NAT2 to 7-acetamido-clonazepam.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced clonazepam exposure; potential breakthrough seizures

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: NAT2 slow acetylators show altered metabolite profile but minor clinical impact.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Anticonvulsant tolerance prominent within weeks-to-months at therapeutic doses (~30–50% of patients lose efficacy). Anxiolytic tolerance slower.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 1–7 days (long t1/2 buffers it); protracted withdrawal common (months). Severe in long-term users; among the more difficult benzos to taper.

notes: Long t1/2 (30–40 h) makes clonazepam useful for sustained anxiolysis/anticonvulsant action but contributes to accumulation and protracted withdrawal.

name: Triazolam

binding.notes: Triazolobenzodiazepine with very high intrinsic activity.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolobenzodiazepine PAM, classical non-selective binding; very high intrinsic efficacy contributes to potent hypnotic effect and prominent anterograde amnesia.

routes.notes: Short t1/2 1.5–5.5 h (mean ~2.3 h). High first-pass.

metabolism.notes: Rapidly glucuronidated → minimal pharmacological contribution. 4-hydroxytriazolam is the minor pathway.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Rapid tolerance to hypnotic effect within 1–2 weeks at typical doses.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Pronounced rebound insomnia within nights of discontinuation (very short t1/2 + high potency). Daytime anxiety, tremor; severe in chronic users.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: CL reduced ~30%, t1/2 prolonged. Maximum recommended dose 0.125 mg.

notes: Highest-potency hypnotic benzo (0.125–0.5 mg dose). Notorious 1980s controversy over psychiatric adverse effects ('Halcion suit'); withdrawn in UK 1991.

name: Flunitrazepam

binding.notes: Used as the canonical radioligand for benzodiazepine binding studies.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: High-affinity non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM. The 1-methyl + 7-nitro motif gives extremely potent sedation/amnesia.

metabolism.notes: Km 108 μM CYP3A4 / 11 μM CYP2C19 — CYP2C19 is the high-affinity contributor at low concentrations.
Nitroreduction by CYP3A4 + nitroreductase; inactive but the primary forensic urinary marker.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs may show higher parent exposure / lower desmethyl formation.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Similar to other intermediate-duration benzos; abuse-related dependence prominent.

notes: Schedule III in US (others IV); reformulated with blue dye to deter DFSA (drug-facilitated sexual assault) use.

name: Oxazepam

binding.notes: Lower potency than diazepam; clinically used as anxiolytic with intermediate t1/2.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM; the 3-hydroxy group eliminates need for CYP-mediated metabolism — directly glucuronidated.

routes.notes: t1/2 3–21 h (mean ~8 h); slowest oral absorption of any benzo (Tmax ~2–4 h).

metabolism.notes: Court 2002 — S-isomer almost exclusively glucuronidated by UGT2B15. R-isomer uses UGT2B7 and UGT1A9.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: UGT2B15 D85Y polymorphism reduces S-oxazepam glucuronidation. Women have longer t1/2 than men.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild relative to short-acting benzos; preferred in elderly alcohol withdrawal.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Preferred benzo in hepatic disease (LOT: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam — no CYP metabolism).

notes: Terminal metabolite of nordazepam pathway (oxazepam is what diazepam ultimately becomes). Marketed as Serax. LOT rule.

name: Temazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM. 3-hydroxy already present → direct glucuronidation, no CYP metabolism needed.

routes.notes: t1/2 8–15 h; intermediate hypnotic duration.

metabolism.notes: Stereoselective: UGT2B7/1A9 dominant for R-temazepam; UGT2B15/1A6 for S-temazepam.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Moderate; rebound insomnia on cessation.

data_gaps_remaining: Subunit-specific Ki not separately characterized; assumed non-selective like other 1,4-benzos
notes: Active metabolite of diazepam; clinically used as standalone hypnotic. LOT rule applies.

name: Nordazepam

binding.notes: Comparable affinity to diazepam; the long-acting backbone of diazepam, prazepam, clorazepate, halazepam metabolism.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Active common metabolite of multiple parent benzos; the long t1/2 (50–100 h) of nordazepam dominates pharmacology on chronic dosing of diazepam, clorazepate, prazepam, etc.

routes.notes: t1/2 50–100 h; accumulates substantially on chronic dosing.

metabolism.notes: 3-hydroxylation → oxazepam → UGT2B15 glucuronidation.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild due to very long t1/2 (acts as self-tapering).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked accumulation; substantial CL reduction.

notes: Marketed alone in France/Italy (Nordaz). Also the active metabolite of diazepam, clorazepate, prazepam, halazepam, medazepam, ketazolam — anything that eventually demethylates to a 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one without N1 substituent.

name: Chlordiazepoxide

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: First benzodiazepine synthesized (Sternbach 1955); 2-methylamino-4-oxide moiety distinguishes it structurally. Metabolized to a cascade of active species (desmethylchlordiazepoxide → demoxepam → nordazepam → oxazepam).

routes.notes: t1/2 5–30 h (mean 12 h); demoxepam t1/2 14–95 h.

metabolism.notes: Demoxepam t1/2 14–95 h; further metabolized to nordazepam → oxazepam.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild due to long-acting active metabolites — preferred for alcohol withdrawal (CIWA protocols).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked CL reduction; metabolite accumulation.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic disease: demoxepam t1/2 up to 346 h reported.

notes: Sternbach's 1955 discovery; first benzodiazepine. Cascade metabolism gives 'self-tapering' withdrawal that suits alcohol detoxification.

name: Librium

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Brand name for chlordiazepoxide. See Chlordiazepoxide record.

notes: Duplicate entry; see Chlordiazepoxide. Recommend deduplication in source data.

name: Bromazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM with pyridyl ring substituting phenyl. Metabolism is unusual for a benzo — mainly CYP1A2 (not CYP3A4).

metabolism.notes: Fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor) ↑ AUC 2.4-fold. Itraconazole (CYP3A4 inhibitor) has no effect → CYP3A4 not involved.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP1A2 inducers (smoking, char-grilled meat) may reduce bromazepam exposure.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Standard moderate-duration benzo withdrawal.

data_gaps_remaining: Specific GABA-A subunit Ki values not separately determined
notes: Unusual among benzos in being metabolized predominantly by CYP1A2 rather than CYP3A4. Marketed primarily outside US (Lexotan/Lexotanil).

name: Clobazam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 1,5-benzodiazepine (rather than 1,4), gives mild α2-subunit preference → relatively less sedation/cognitive impairment than diazepam at equipotent anxiolytic doses. Anticonvulsant for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (Onfi FDA approval 2011).

routes.notes: Clobazam t1/2 36–42 h; N-desmethylclobazam (norclobazam) t1/2 71–82 h.

metabolism.notes: ~2/3 of clobazam undergoes N-demethylation. Norclobazam is ~25% as potent but at chronic dosing reaches plasma concentrations 8–20× clobazam.
CYP2C19 PMs have 5× higher norclobazam levels — clinically important for dosing in Asian populations.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Norclobazam levels 2–3× higher; clinically significant in Dravet syndrome co-treatment
Norclobazam AUC increased ~3–4×; major clinical interaction in Lennox-Gastaut and Dravet co-treatment

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs: norclobazam plasma levels 5× higher than EMs; recommend lower starting dose. ~15% of East Asians are CYP2C19 PMs.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Anticonvulsant tolerance develops in ~30% within 6 months.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild relative to 1,4-benzos but can precipitate status in epileptic patients; long t1/2 buffers it.

notes: Structural outlier among benzos (1,5- rather than 1,4-). Lower sedation per equipotent anxiolytic dose. Norclobazam carries most of the chronic-dosing effect.

name: Zopiclone

binding.notes: Racemic mixture; S-enantiomer (eszopiclone) is ~50× more active.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cyclopyrrolone PAM. Racemate; almost all activity resides in S-enantiomer (eszopiclone). Non-selective like classical benzos.

routes.notes: t1/2 5 h; not approved in US (eszopiclone marketed instead).

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Comparable to short-acting benzos; rebound insomnia common.

off_targets.target: Unidentified salivary excretion → bitter taste receptor
off_targets.clinical_consequence: Characteristic metallic/bitter aftertaste (dysgeusia) due to salivary excretion of the parent drug.

notes: Racemic version of eszopiclone; activity dominated by S-enantiomer. Not approved in US.

name: Sonata

binding.notes: Brand: Sonata; generic name zaleplon. Dämgen & Lüddens 1999: 12-, 10-, 27× selective for α1 vs α2, α3, α5 respectively — most α1-selective of the Z-drugs.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pyrazolopyrimidine PAM. Greatest α1 selectivity among Z-drugs → almost pure hypnotic, with minimal anxiolytic/myorelaxant activity. Ultra-short t1/2 (~1 h) makes it suited for sleep-onset insomnia.

routes.notes: Very short t1/2 ~1 h. Extensive first-pass via aldehyde oxidase (not CYP).

metabolism.notes: Unusual: primary clearance is via aldehyde oxidase, not CYP. Minimal CYP interactions.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: AUC decreased ~80% (despite minor CYP3A4 contribution, induction is substantial)

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Minimal at therapeutic doses due to ultra-short t1/2; rare rebound insomnia.

demographic_differences.sex: Females: AUC 30–45% higher; dose adjustment advised.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: CL reduced ~70%; max recommended 5 mg.

notes: Most α1-selective Z-drug. Aldehyde oxidase metabolism is unusual — gives different DDI profile than CYP-metabolized Z-drugs.

name: Flurazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Parent compound has short t1/2 (2–3 h); virtually all clinical effect mediated by N-desalkylflurazepam (norflurazepam), t1/2 47–150 h (mean ~71 h).

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 2.3 h; active metabolite N-desalkylflurazepam dominates effect.

metabolism.notes: t1/2 47–150 h; accumulates with chronic dosing.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild due to long-acting metabolite; significant daytime sedation hangover on initiation.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked accumulation of norflurazepam; avoid.

notes: Effectively a prodrug; all chronic effect mediated by N-desalkylflurazepam (= norflurazepam).

name: Quazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Unusual α1-preferring classical benzodiazepine. 2-thione group (not 2-oxo). Both parent and 2-oxoquazepam metabolite are α1-selective. Distal metabolite N-desalkyl-2-oxoquazepam is non-selective and long-lived.

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 ~36 h; N-desalkyl-2-oxoquazepam t1/2 ~70 h.

metabolism.notes: Identical to N-desalkylflurazepam in structure — long-acting common metabolite.

data_gaps_remaining: Subunit-specific Ki not published in detail
notes: Only commercial benzo claiming α1 selectivity; clinical advantage modest because the major metabolite is non-selective and long-lived.

name: Estazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolobenzodiazepine without methyl on the triazolo ring (cf. alprazolam, triazolam which both have 1-methyl).

data_gaps_remaining: Specific subunit Ki not in literature
notes: Triazolobenzodiazepine hypnotic — intermediate t1/2 between triazolam and alprazolam. Withdrawn from many markets.

name: Clorazepate

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug: rapidly decarboxylated to nordazepam in acidic gastric environment (chemical hydrolysis, not enzymatic). All pharmacology mediated by nordazepam.

routes.notes: Parent not detected systemically; nordazepam t1/2 50–100 h.

metabolism.notes: Decarboxylation requires acidic pH — antacids/PPIs can reduce conversion and onset.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Slower onset and reduced peak nordazepam levels

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Inherited via nordazepam — CYP2C19 PMs accumulate more.

notes: Prodrug — nordazepam carries all activity. Reduced gastric acidity impairs conversion.

name: Prazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug — N-dealkylated by CYP3A4 to nordazepam. Smoother onset than diazepam.

routes.notes: Effect via nordazepam; t1/2 50–100 h.

notes: Prodrug for nordazepam, like clorazepate.

name: Halazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug — N-dealkylated to nordazepam.

notes: Discontinued in most markets; pharmacology essentially that of nordazepam.

name: Medazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug — metabolized to diazepam, nordazepam, and finally oxazepam. Lacks 2-oxo group of diazepam.

notes: Prodrug — metabolized to diazepam then nordazepam.

name: Lormetazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 1-methyl analogue of lorazepam (lorazepam + methyl on N1); 3-OH → direct glucuronidation.

metabolism.notes: Minor N-demethylation to lorazepam.

notes: Like lorazepam plus N1-methyl; mostly glucuronidated; hepatic-disease-friendly.

name: Brotizolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienotriazolodiazepine — like etizolam structurally. Very potent hypnotic.

notes: Marketed in Japan/Europe (Lendormin); not US.

name: Etizolam

binding.notes: Sanna et al. 2005. Higher affinity than alprazolam (7.9 nM).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienotriazolodiazepine — replaces benzo ring with thiophene. Sanna 2005 reports lower Emax than alprazolam at α1, hypothesized to underlie its 'lower tolerance liability' (a contested claim in the recreational use literature).

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 ~3.4 h; α-hydroxyetizolam t1/2 ~8 h.

metabolism.notes: α-hydroxyetizolam is active and has longer t1/2 (~8 h) than parent. Major urinary forensic marker.
Minor contribution.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Sanna 2005 reported lower tolerance liability in rats vs alprazolam (less receptor uncoupling); human data on chronic use show robust tolerance and dependence.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe in heavy/long-term recreational use — comparable to alprazolam withdrawal: anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity, seizures.

notes: Schedule IV in Japan/Italy/India (legitimate Rx); scheduled or controlled in most other Western countries. Bridge compound between classical benzos and designer benzos — was prescribed for decades before becoming a major NPS in 2010s.

name: Phenazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Soviet-developed (1970s) 1,4-benzodiazepine; reported in Russian literature as 5–10× more potent than diazepam. Both phenazepam and 3-OH-phenazepam are pharmacologically active.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~60 h in healthy adults; 15–60 h range. Tmax ~4 h. Effects last up to 5 days; some case reports describe symptoms up to 3 weeks post-ingestion.

metabolism.notes: 3-OH-phenazepam is active but in humans plasma levels are very low (<3 ng/mL) — minimal contribution. Subsequently glucuronidated.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Protracted due to very long t1/2 (60+ h). Severe in chronic users — comparable to long-acting benzos but with potency that allows easy overdose.

data_gaps_remaining: Specific subunit Ki not published; assumed non-selective like other 1,4-benzos
notes: Originally developed in USSR 1970s as an anxiolytic/anticonvulsant; emerged as a major NPS in Europe 2007 onward. Among the longest-t1/2 benzodiazepines and a notable post-mortem-finding NPS.

name: 3-Hydroxyphenazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Active hydroxy metabolite of phenazepam, sold as standalone designer benzo. Like other 3-OH-benzos (oxazepam, lorazepam), bypasses CYP — direct glucuronidation.

data_gaps_remaining: Specific human PK with this compound as the parent administered
notes: Active metabolite of phenazepam, sold separately as a designer benzo (sometimes labelled '3-OH-P' or '3-OH-phenazepam'). Equipotent to phenazepam by Russian-literature accounts.

name: 3-oh-phenazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Alias of 3-Hydroxyphenazepam. See that record.

notes: Duplicate entry of 3-Hydroxyphenazepam — recommend deduplication.

name: Flubromazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 1,4-benzodiazepine designer benzo with 7-bromo + 2'-fluoro substitution; long-acting like phenazepam. Predicted GABA-A Ki similar to diazepam by QSAR (Manchester 2022).

routes.notes: Moosmann 2013 self-experiment. t1/2 ~106 h. Detection in urine for 28 days, serum for 23 days.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Very prolonged — t1/2 >100 h means clinical effects can extend 3+ weeks per single dose.

notes: Extremely long t1/2 (106 h) — among the longest of any benzodiazepine. 4 mg dose produces detectable serum levels for nearly a month.

name: Flubromazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolobenzodiazepine — alprazolam analogue with 8-bromo + 2'-fluoro substitution. Predicted GABA-A binding affinity exceptionally high (log 1/c ~10 by Manchester 2022 QSAR). High intrinsic activity contributes to rapid tolerance.

routes.notes: Huppertz 2018 self-experiment, 0.5 mg. t1/2 ~10–20 h. Detection in urine up to 8 days.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Triazolobenzodiazepines (alprazolam-class) show especially rapid tolerance and severe withdrawal.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe even at low cumulative doses; multiple post-mortem cases reported.

data_gaps_remaining: Population PK; subunit Ki not published
notes: Active oral dose 0.25–0.5 mg — among the most potent benzodiazepines synthesized. Post-mortem-case-series subject in 5+ studies (Hikin/Abdul 2020, Lewis 2019). Rat PK studies show ~2× larger Vd and CL vs alprazolam (doi:10.1016/j.taap.2023.116481).

name: Clonazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolam + 7-nitro group (combines triazolam scaffold with clonazepam's nitro substitution). Among the most potent benzodiazepines; active at 0.1–0.5 mg.

metabolism.notes: Parallel to clonazepam nitroreduction.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe; triazolo + nitro structure gives both high intrinsic activity and prolonged tail.

notes: First synthesized 1971 (Hester); appeared as NPS ~2014. Recreational doses 0.25–1 mg. Notorious for blackouts, paradoxical disinhibition, and acute respiratory depression risk when combined with opioids/alcohol.

name: Flualprazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Alprazolam with 2'-fluoro substitution on phenyl. Predicted GABA-A affinity exceptionally high by Manchester QSAR (log 1/c 10.13). Roughly twice the t1/2 of alprazolam in rat PK studies.

routes.subject_demographics: Estimated from rat PK + post-mortem cases (Rice/Hikin 2019)
routes.notes: Rat PK: Vd and CL ~2× alprazolam; t1/2 ~2× longer (extrapolation to human ~18 h).

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe — comparable to alprazolam but t1/2 nearly doubled.

notes: Major designer benzo of late 2010s. Nine-case post-mortem series by Rice & Hikin 2019; deaths involved poly-drug intoxication, none attributed to flualprazolam alone.

name: Bromazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Alprazolam's 8-bromo analogue (vs 8-chloro). Synthesized 1976 (Hester) but never marketed. Late-2010s/2020s NPS — increasingly common in North American post-mortem case series, often as a fentanyl adulterant.

notes: Emerged as a major opioid adulterant in 2022–2024 North American drug supply. Increasingly detected in overdose deaths. CFSRE NPS Discovery monitoring shows >300% increase 2022–2023.

name: Diclazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 2'-chlorodiazepam designer benzo. Like diazepam, metabolism produces active metabolites: delorazepam (N-demethylation), and the unusual case of hydroxylation producing lorazepam/lormetazepam.

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 ~42 h. Active metabolites delorazepam (detectable 6 days), lorazepam (19 days), lormetazepam (11 days).

metabolism.notes: Unusual: diclazepam metabolism converges with several marketed benzo metabolites.

notes: Notable for producing lorazepam and lormetazepam as active metabolites in vivo. Confounds urine drug testing (positive for prescription benzos).

name: Adinazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolobenzodiazepine prodrug — N-desmethyladinazolam (NDMAD) is ~25× more potent at benzodiazepine receptors than parent. Extensive first-pass conversion.

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 ~2.9 h, NDMAD t1/2 ~2.8 h; elderly: +40%.

metabolism.notes: >80% of dose converted to NDMAD. Affinity for benzodiazepine receptors is ~25× parent's.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: t1/2 +40% for both parent and NDMAD.

notes: Developed by Upjohn 1970s as 'Deracyn' antidepressant; never marketed. Re-emerged as a designer benzo. Effectively a prodrug for NDMAD.

name: Pyrazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolobenzodiazepine with 2-pyridyl (like bromazepam) replacing 2-chlorophenyl of alprazolam. Some literature suggests α2/α3 selectivity but data are sparse. Distinct in that it does NOT undergo Phase I metabolism — directly glucuronidated.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~17 h. Unique among designer benzos in being directly glucuronidated (no Phase I).

metabolism.notes: Unusual — pyrazolam is excreted largely as parent + glucuronide; no hydroxy metabolites detected.

notes: First designer benzo to enter the NPS market (~2012). Unique: no Phase I metabolism — direct glucuronidation makes it CYP-interaction-resistant.

name: Nifoxipam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 3-hydroxy-desmethylflunitrazepam. Active metabolite of flunitrazepam sold as designer benzo. 3-OH group → direct glucuronidation (no CYP needed).

notes: Active metabolite of flunitrazepam sold separately. 3-OH structure means lorazepam-like metabolism.

name: Desmethylflunitrazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-desmethyl metabolite of flunitrazepam (= norflunitrazepam = fonazepam) sold as standalone NPS. Some intrinsic activity at GABA-A.

notes: Aliases include fonazepam, norflunitrazepam, Ro05-4435. Active metabolite of flunitrazepam.

name: 4'-chlorodiazepam

binding.notes: Selective TSPO agonist; lacks affinity for central GABA-A benzodiazepine site.
No clinically meaningful GABA-A activity. Behaviorally distinct from typical benzodiazepines.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Selective TSPO (mitochondrial 18 kDa translocator) agonist. Modulates steroidogenesis (cholesterol → pregnenolone via cytochrome P450scc); investigated for neuroprotection. NOT a classical benzodiazepine despite the name.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Negligible classical benzodiazepine activity — does not function as a sedative/anxiolytic.

notes: Critical distinction: despite the name and benzodiazepine scaffold, Ro5-4864 is a TSPO agonist research compound — not a GABAergic anxiolytic. Suppresses mast cell pro-inflammatory function. Investigated for neuroprotection. Should be flagged distinctly from classical benzos in any harm-reduction database.

name: 4-chlorodiazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Alias of 4'-chlorodiazepam (Ro5-4864). See that record. NOT a classical benzodiazepine.

notes: Duplicate of 4'-chlorodiazepam; recommend deduplication. The 'GABAA-PAM' tag is incorrect — this compound does not act on GABA-A.

name: Avizafone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Water-soluble peptidic prodrug of diazepam — L-lysyl-substituted, cleaved by plasma aminopeptidases. Designed for IM/IV bioterrorism antidote use (nerve-agent-induced status epilepticus). All pharmacology = diazepam.

routes.notes: Rapidly converted to diazepam within minutes of IM injection. Faster than IM diazepam (poor IM absorption) due to water solubility.

notes: Water-soluble diazepam prodrug developed by Roche; used in French/UK military auto-injectors for organophosphate nerve-agent treatment.

name: Rilmazafone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Water-soluble peptide prodrug. Aminopeptidases in small intestine cleave the glycyl side chain → ring closure → active triazolobenzodiazepine (8-chloro-6-(2-chlorophenyl)-N,N-dimethyl-4H-triazolo[1,5-a][1,4]benzodiazepine-2-carboxamide).

routes.notes: Parent has no benzodiazepine receptor activity; active metabolite t1/2 ~10 h.

notes: Marketed in Japan as Rhythmy hypnotic; developed by Shionogi. Pharmacologically distinct from avizafone in that the metabolite is a novel triazolobenzodiazepine rather than diazepam.

name: Delorazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-desmethyl metabolite of diclazepam. Italian-marketed long-acting anxiolytic (EN, Dadumir).

routes.notes: t1/2 50–100 h (very long); active metabolite lorazepam via 3-hydroxylation.

notes: Marketed in Italy; metabolite of diclazepam. Also called nordiclazepam or chlordesmethyldiazepam.

name: Norflurazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-desalkylflurazepam = norflurazepam. Long-acting active metabolite of flurazepam and quazepam; sold as a designer benzo. t1/2 47–150 h.

notes: Identical to N-desalkylflurazepam. Active metabolite of flurazepam (Dalmane) and quazepam (Doral).

name: Clotiazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienodiazepine (like etizolam structurally). Used in Japan/Italy/France as a short-acting anxiolytic.

notes: Thienodiazepine sister to etizolam; widely marketed in Japan (Rize, Trecalmo).

name: Bentazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienodiazepine. Spanish-marketed (Tiadipona). QSAR-predicted GABA-A log 1/c 6.88 (low end for class) per Manchester 2022.

notes: Marketed in Spain only (Tiadipona); withdrawn from many markets due to hepatotoxicity reports.

name: Cinolazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Austrian-marketed hypnotic (Gerodorm). Pre-drug-like — 3-hydroxylated to active metabolite.

notes: Marketed in Austria; minor benzodiazepine hypnotic.

name: Cloxazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Oxazolam-type prodrug — opens the oxazoline ring to release delorazepam.

notes: Oxazolobenzodiazepine prodrug.

name: Oxazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Oxazolobenzodiazepine prodrug — releases nordazepam upon gastric hydrolysis.

notes: Japanese-marketed (Serenal); prodrug.

name: Ketazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Oxazinobenzodiazepine prodrug — opens to diazepam, then nordazepam.

notes: Prodrug of diazepam.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Oxazolobenzodiazepine. Portuguese/Brazilian marketed (Sedoxil, Melex).
Bromo-substituted benzodiazepine, German-marketed (Talis). N-demethylation → desmethylmetaclazepam active metabolite.

name: Tetrazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cyclohexene-substituted benzodiazepine marketed as a muscle relaxant. EMA suspended marketing in 2013 due to serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN).

notes: EMA suspended 2013 due to risk of severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Imidazolobenzodiazepine hypnotic (UK/French Dormonoct).
Japanese-marketed (Coleminal); N-hydroxyethyl analogue. Metabolized to N-desalkyl-flutazolam.

name: Flutoprazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Japanese long-acting anxiolytic (Restas). N-cyclopropylmethyl substitution.

notes: Japan only.

name: Nimetazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Japanese-marketed (Erimin); structurally between nitrazepam and flunitrazepam. Major NPS in SE Asia.

notes: Major NPS in Malaysia, Singapore, Hong Kong as 'Erimin-5'.

name: Nitemazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 3-hydroxynimetazepam; active metabolite sold as designer benzo.

notes: 3-hydroxy metabolite of nimetazepam.

name: Nitrazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Nitro-substituted triazolobenzodiazepine; designer benzo with potency between nitrazepam and clonazolam.

notes: Designer benzo with combined triazolo + nitro features.

name: Flunitrazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolo + nitro + fluoro — combines features of flunitrazepam and clonazolam. Extreme potency expected.

notes: Designer benzo, active oral dose reported ~0.1 mg. Insufficient peer-reviewed PK.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienotriazolodiazepine. QSAR-predicted log 1/c 8.91 (Manchester 2022).

name: Fluetizolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Fluoro-etizolam; thienotriazolodiazepine designer benzo.

notes: Designer benzo; sparse peer-reviewed data.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Etizolam without 2'-chloro on phenyl. Reduced potency vs etizolam (~10× less).
Desmethyletizolam = metizolam — etizolam analogue with methyl in place of ethyl. Reduced potency.

name: Meclonazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: (S)-3-methylclonazepam. Originally developed as anti-schistosomal; never marketed for that. Active (S)-enantiomer; designer benzo.

notes: Developed as anti-schistosomal. Hester 1971 patent.

name: Cloniprazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-cyclopropylmethyl clonazepam analogue; designer benzo.

notes: Sparse data; community-reported potent.

name: Clobromazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Combination of 2'-Cl + 8-Br + triazolo features → predicted very high GABA-A affinity (QSAR log 1/c 10.14, Manchester 2022). Among most-monitored designer benzos by EMCDDA post-2017.

notes: Synonymous with 'Phenazolam' as vendor name. EMCDDA monitoring since 2018.

name: Phenazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Vendor name for clobromazolam — see that record.

notes: Duplicate of clobromazolam — recommend deduplication.

name: Gidazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Ukrainian-developed anxiolytic. Hydrazide prodrug → bromonordiazepam (active, long t1/2).

notes: Ukrainian/Russian prescription anxiolytic. Active metabolite bromonordiazepam itself has emerged as a designer benzo (desalkylgidazepam).

name: Zolazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pyrazolodiazepine; used in veterinary anaesthesia (Telazol/Zoletil = tiletamine + zolazepam combination).

notes: Veterinary use — Telazol/Zoletil combination with tiletamine.

shared_mechanism: All compounds are positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) at the GABA-A receptor benzodiazepine binding site, located at the α/γ subunit interface (α+ side, γ2- side). Binding enhances GABA-induced Cl- channel opening frequency at GABA-bound receptors, hyperpolarising neurons. Pharmacological subunit selectivity defines clinical/recreational profile: α1-containing GABA-A receptors mediate sedation, anterograde amnesia, ataxia, and reinforcement (abuse liability); α2/α3-containing receptors mediate anxiolysis and muscle relaxation; α5-containing receptors mediate cognitive effects (memory, learning). Classical 1,4-benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, clonazepam) bind α1/α2/α3/α5 with roughly equal nanomolar affinity. Zolpidem and zaleplon are α1-preferring (>20× vs other subtypes); eszopiclone is non-selective like classical benzos. The benzodiazepine site has no GABA-A receptor-mediated activity in the absence of GABA — these are not direct agonists. The closely related TSPO ('peripheral benzodiazepine receptor') is structurally distinct and not GABA-A; compounds like Ro5-4864 (4'-chlorodiazepam) bind TSPO selectively and produce no benzodiazepine-like effects.
shared_pk_summary: Most classical benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, triazolam, midazolam, flunitrazepam, clobazam) are CYP3A4 substrates (some additionally CYP2C19, especially diazepam and flunitrazepam). The 'LOT' rule — lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam — identifies benzos cleared by direct UGT2B7/UGT2B15 glucuronidation without Phase I metabolism, making them preferred in hepatic impairment and resistant to CYP-mediated drug-drug interactions. Active metabolites dominate the clinical pharmacology of multiple parent compounds: diazepam → nordazepam (t1/2 50–100 h) → oxazepam; flurazepam/quazepam → N-desalkylflurazepam (norflurazepam, t1/2 47–150 h); alprazolam → α-hydroxyalprazolam; midazolam → 1-OH-midazolam (~20% potency); clobazam → norclobazam (8–20× plasma vs parent on chronic dosing). Plasma protein binding is generally 80–97%, dominated by albumin. Volume of distribution 0.5–3 L/kg (lipid-soluble). Z-drugs zolpidem and zaleplon have very short t1/2 (1.5–3 h) and are 80–95% protein-bound. Pyrazolam is unusual in having NO Phase I metabolism (direct glucuronidation only). Designer benzos with very long t1/2 include flubromazepam (~106 h), diclazepam (~42 h), and phenazepam (~60 h) — these dramatically prolong effects of single doses to weeks. CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit juice) markedly elevate exposure of CYP3A4-cleared benzos; inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) markedly reduce it.
shared_safety: The signal harm of benzodiazepines is RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION when combined with other CNS depressants — especially opioids, alcohol, GHB/GBL, and Z-drugs themselves. Alone, benzodiazepines are remarkably non-lethal: documented LD50 ratios are extraordinary (the original Roche estimates put diazepam's LD50/ED50 at >100). Almost all benzodiazepine-attributed deaths involve concurrent CNS depressants. The 2010s/2020s overdose epidemic in North America/Europe with designer benzos (clonazolam, flualprazolam, bromazolam) overwhelmingly involves co-ingestion of fentanyl or its analogues. Specific risks: (1) anterograde amnesia (more pronounced with triazolam, alprazolam, midazolam, flunitrazepam → DFSA potential); (2) paradoxical disinhibition / behavioural disinhibition (~1–2% incidence, more common in elderly, children, alcoholics, those with personality disorders); (3) physical dependence and withdrawal, with seizure risk on abrupt cessation from high doses of short-acting compounds (alprazolam, triazolam, oxazepam) — withdrawal can be fatal without taper; (4) increased fall/fracture risk in elderly; (5) cognitive impairment with chronic use; (6) tolerance to anticonvulsant/hypnotic effects more rapid than to anxiolytic effects. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site and reverses sedation acutely (1–2 h duration); not used in chronic users because it can precipitate withdrawal seizures. Z-drugs additionally carry a recognized risk of complex sleep-related behaviours (sleep-driving, sleep-eating, sleep-sex) prompting an FDA boxed warning in 2019 for zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone.
sar_summary: Core 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one scaffold: 7-substituent on the fused benzene determines potency (7-Cl in diazepam, 7-Br in phenazepam/flubromazepam → more potent than unsubstituted; 7-NO2 in clonazepam/flunitrazepam/nitrazepam → very high affinity); 5-aryl group is essential (phenyl = standard; 2'-Cl in lorazepam/clonazepam/diclazepam → potency boost; 2'-F in flunitrazepam/midazolam → metabolic stability + potency; 2-pyridyl in bromazepam/pyrazolam → different metabolic fate). N1-substitution: H = standard (nordazepam); methyl (diazepam) → modest change; 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl (halazepam, quazepam) → α1-selectivity hint; diethylaminoethyl (flurazepam) → prodrug-like, parent inactive, all activity from N-dealkylation. 3-position: 3-OH (oxazepam, lorazepam, temazepam, lormetazepam) → bypasses CYP, direct glucuronidation, no active metabolites, hepatic-safe; 3-methyl (meclonazepam) → adds stereochemistry. RING MODIFICATIONS: triazolo-annulation [1,2,4-triazolo[4,3-a]] (alprazolam, triazolam, estazolam, clonazolam, flubromazolam, flualprazolam, bromazolam, adinazolam) → markedly increases intrinsic activity at the benzodiazepine site → higher potency, faster tolerance, more severe withdrawal; thieno-replacement of the benzene (etizolam, brotizolam, clotiazepam, deschloroetizolam, metizolam) → thienodiazepine, faster onset, slightly different binding kinetics; 1,5-benzodiazepine ring rearrangement (clobazam) → mild α2-preference, less sedation. PRO-DRUGS exploit aminopeptidase cleavage (avizafone → diazepam; rilmazafone → triazolobenzodiazepine metabolite) or gastric chemical hydrolysis (clorazepate → nordazepam; ketazolam → diazepam; oxazolam → nordazepam) or CYP-mediated N-dealkylation (prazepam → nordazepam; flurazepam → norflurazepam; quazepam → 2-oxoquazepam; medazepam → diazepam). Z-DRUGS occupy the benzodiazepine site without sharing the benzo scaffold: imidazopyridine (zolpidem, α1-preferring), pyrazolopyrimidine (zaleplon, highly α1-preferring), cyclopyrrolone (zopiclone/eszopiclone, non-selective like classical benzos). The α1G201 residue (Pritchett & Seeburg 1991) is the structural determinant for zolpidem's α1 selectivity. TSPO ligands (Ro5-4864 = 4'-chlorodiazepam) share the benzodiazepine scaffold but bind a structurally unrelated mitochondrial protein and have no GABA-A activity.
